notes: The vocative Maa fixes the addressee as the speaker's own mother; tum vs aap is a household/mood choice (a child who normally says tum may shift to aap when being deferential or pleading), so both can be said to the same mother. aaogi/aayengi is agreement forced by the pronoun.

Papa is a unique addressee; tum+kha lo vs aap+kha lijiye is a register shift the same child makes, e.g. casually at the table vs coaxing a tired father to eat. lo/lijiye is the imperative form each pronoun selects, not an independent change.

Intimate tu to one's mother is common in many North Indian (esp. Punjabi/Haryanvi-influenced) households and in emotional reassurance; the same child can alternate tu/tum with the same Maa. kar/karo is forced agreement.

ambiguity_reason: Didi covers both one's own elder sister (often addressed with tu) and non-kin respected elder women (teacher, senior, neighbour; addressed with aap), and the jump from tu straight to aap is large enough that the pair could signal either one sister or two different 'didis'.
notes: Tu with Didi is common between close-in-age sisters, so a is natural; the two-step tu->aap shift plus the fictive use of Didi leaves the referent question open. rahi hai/rahi hain is forced agreement.

Nani (maternal grandmother) is a single fixed person; grandchildren who are close to her often use tum, and the same grandchild may switch to aap when urging her to take medicine. le lo/le lijiye is the pronoun-matched imperative.
Same father addressed; tum with Papa is ordinary in many urban families and aap in others, and one speaker can mix them across a conversation about his Delhi trip. ja rahe ho/hain is agreement.

tumne/aapne is the only change and the ergative verb dekha stays constant; a child asking Papa about their result could naturally use either form to the same father depending on how anxious/formal they feel.
Asking Maa whether she has eaten is a routine caring question; the same child uses tumne or aapne to the same mother, with no other change (khaya unchanged under ergative).

ambiguity_reason: Chef as a vocative is used both for one's actual boss (du in du-culture firms, Sie traditionally) and jocularly for strangers such as waiters or tradesmen, so the T-V switch could reflect two different addressees or a context shift that cannot be resolved in isolation.
notes: hast du/haben Sie is the only change (verb agreement forced). German T-V is normally stable within a dyad, but the flexible use of Chef as an address term prevents a confident call.

Asking the boss to read a report by Friday is a fixed workplace context; within a German employee-boss dyad du or Sie is agreed once and kept, so the two forms most plausibly reflect two different bosses (a du-culture boss vs a Sie boss). kannst/können is forced agreement.

First name + Sie ('Hamburger Sie') is acceptable in offices, but a given speaker settles on du or Sie with a given Lena; a first name alone does not pin down one person, so the T-V choice signals two distinct Lenas (e.g. a friend vs a client/trainee). hast/haben is agreement.

b is unnatural: thanking someone for help with a house move (typically a close-friend favour) using first name + Ihre is an odd combination. German speakers do not alternate deine/Ihre for the same Thomas, so the forms point to different helpers (friend vs e.g. a neighbour on Sie terms).

ambiguity_reason: The highly specific event (the boss's 60th birthday) suggests a single referent, while the stable German T-V choice suggests two different speaker-boss relationships, and nothing in the pair decides between them.
notes: deinem/Ihrem is the only change. Duzen a boss is normal in du-culture firms and Siezen elsewhere; with no context it is unclear whether this is one boss or two.

Markus + dein vs Ihr: small talk about an Italy holiday happens with both colleagues and clients, but one speaker keeps a fixed T-V form with one Markus; the choice most plausibly marks a du-colleague vs a first-name-Sie business contact.

Praise for a presentation from a peer (du) vs a manager or instructor who addresses Sabine with first name + Sie; since T-V is stable per dyad, the two forms signal two different Sabine relationships, i.e. most plausibly two Sabines. du hast/Sie haben is agreement.

Asking Jonas to pick you up from the station is a personal favour typical of a du relationship; with Sie it reads as addressing a service provider (e.g. a driver called by first name). The register signals different addressees. kannst/können is agreement.
The -어/-어요 ending indexes the listener, not the referent: the same speaker reports the same call from Mom as 전화했어 to a sibling and 전화했어요 to a teacher. Only the sentence ending differs.
우리 형 (the male speaker's elder brother) is the same person in both; the speaker says 결혼했어 to a friend and 결혼했어요 to a senior colleague. Speech level only concerns the addressee.
Subject honorific -시- (오셨-) is held constant for 할머니 in both; only the listener-oriented ending changes, e.g. telling a younger cousin vs one's aunt that the same Grandma arrived.
Same Dad, same car purchase; 샀어 to a peer and 샀어요 to a neighbour or teacher. No other change.
The referent is the speaker's own dog; 아파 vs 아파요 depends only on whether one tells a friend or the vet/an elder. Clearly the same dog.

내 -> 제 co-varies with the polite ending as part of the same register choice (listed in the distinction value), so treated as minimal, though 제 is not strictly obligatory with -요. Same sibling, same exam: the speaker tells a friend with 내/-어 and a professor with 제/-어요.

At a hospital or care home, staff tell the elderly patient 아드님이 오셨어요 and tell each other 아들이 왔어요 about the very same visitor, a natural same-referent scenario. -시- is agreement forced by the honorific noun.

With no possessor, 딸이 결혼했어요 reads by default as the speaker's own daughter, whereas 따님 can never refer to one's own child and signals the listener's or a third party's daughter; as an isolated wedding announcement the pair points to two daughters. -시- is forced agreement.

아들이 대학에 합격했어요 is the typical parent sharing their own son's news; 아드님이 합격하셨어요 congratulates someone else on their son (the -시- on a student is standard deference to the parent, not odd). The honorific noun reliably excludes the speaker's own son.

ambiguity_reason: A phone-message context supports both readings: a caller's own daughter (a) vs a client's daughter (b), or one daughter reported to a colleague (a) and to her parent (b), and nothing in the pair decides.
notes: 딸/따님 plus the -시- it triggers is the only change. A receptionist could plausibly produce both about the same caller, but the default bare-noun reading is 'my daughter'.

아내 without a possessor is how a man refers to his own wife, while 부인 + -시- is reserved for someone else's wife and is never used for one's own; referring to a superior's wife as 아내 would be inappropriate, so no natural same-referent scenario exists. The noun swap is the target feature itself.
Moving to Seoul: bare 딸 defaults to the speaker's own daughter, and 따님 + 이사하셨어요 marks the addressee's or a third party's daughter, so in isolation the forms signal two different daughters.

ji is an optional respect/affection particle on a kin term; the same grandchild says 'Dadi ji' in front of guests and plain 'Dadi' at home about the same grandmother telling a story. Ergative sunayi is unchanged.

Having a puja performed is a formal household event where 'Dadi ji' is especially likely, but the same speaker refers to the same paternal grandmother as 'Dadi' in casual retelling; ji does not change the referent.
Nani is one's mother's mother, a single person; mentioning that she sent pickle with or without ji is just a politeness choice by the same speaker (e.g. to a guest vs a sibling).
Same maternal grandmother knitting a sweater; ji-marking varies with audience and formality, not with who the grandmother is. Only 'ji' differs.
Dada ji vs Dada about grandpa reading the newspaper: the same grandson alternates freely; ji adds deference without implying a different grandfather.

Nana ji/Nana for the maternal grandfather who bought the bicycle; the same speaker would say 'Nana ji ne cycle dilayi' to a teacher and 'Nana ne' to a friend. dilayi agrees with feminine cycle in both.

uncle (parent's generation) vs bhaiya (elder-sibling generation) with the same surname typically picks out different members of the Gupta household, e.g. the father vs his son; one speaker does not call the same man both at once.

b is slightly unnatural: didi is usually attached to a first name ('Neha didi'), surname + didi ('Sharma didi') is uncommon, while 'Sharma aunty' is idiomatic. The generational terms point to different Sharma women (mother vs daughter).
'Verma uncle' and 'Verma bhaiya' are the classic way to tell apart the older and younger Verma men in a neighbourhood; the generational fictive-kin term signals two different visitors.

b is slightly unnatural (surname + didi is rarer than first name + didi). aunty vs didi encodes the referent's generation relative to the speaker, so the party invitation comes from two different Kapoor women.
'Singh bhaiya' (e.g. an older neighbourhood boy or young tutor) and 'Singh uncle' (a parent-age neighbour/teacher) are distinct people for the same speaker; surname + bhaiya is idiomatic here.

b is slightly unnatural: 'Mishra didi' with a surname is less idiomatic than 'Mishra aunty'. aunty vs didi marks generation, so the food was sent by different Mishra women (e.g. mother vs daughter-in-law/daughter).
